newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court hears abortion protest argument.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court hears abortion protest argument.

text.p: Lawyers for the Justice Department and an abortion-rights group sought on Wednesday to convince a sceptical Supreme Court that restrictions on protesters at abortion clinics in New York had been justified.

The two attorneys argued that the injunction -- which banned demonstrators within 15 feet of the clinics and also required that they stay 15 feet away from anyone who does not want to talk to them -- did not infringe free-speech rights.
They said the 1992 restrictions had been necessary because protesters previously engaged in a campaign to harass abortion-seeking women and obstruct access to the clinics in Buffalo and Rochester.

But a lawyer for two protesters attacked the restrictions as too broad, affecting activities protected by the First Amendment's free-speech guarantees, including demonstrations, picketing and handing out leaflets.

The justices during the hour-long session questioned all three lawyers vigorously, but seemed especially troubled by the floating, 15-foot zone that "sidewalk counsellors" must maintain. A ruling is expected next year.
Physically blocking access to abortion clinics has been a popular tactic of militant factions within the anti-abortion movement, often leading to violent clashes.

Lucinda Finley, a law professor representing the Pro-Choice Network of Western New York, said the defendants had engaged in an "unrelenting campaign" of harassment, trespassing and obstructing the clinics.
She said they had been found to have grabbed, shoved, punched and even knocked people down, making the restrictions necessary. "From 15 feet away, they can communicate," Finley said.
But Justice David Souter questioned the use of moving zones for counsellors, saying they can be difficult to enforce. With a fixed requirement, he said, "Everybody will know what the line is."
Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger of the Justice Department said the judge in crafting the injunction sought to stop "crowding and intimidating" behaviour.
But Justice Anthony Kennedy said the injunction could not prohibit conduct based on speech and must be precisely written. "That's a very difficult First Amendment case," he said.
Both Dellinger and Finley said the restrictions helped women patients avoid stress and possible complications right before a serious medical procedure.
But Justice Antonin Scalia ridiculed the argument, asking whether labour picketing involving air traffic controllers could also be banned to avoid upsetting them.
Jay Sekulow, representing the two protesters, said, "This is not a case involving mass blockades." He added, "We think the debate should tip in favour of free speech here."
But Justice Stephen Breyer from the bench pointed out the justices were more than 15 feet away from the attorneys and still able to communicate.

Sekulow replied that the protesters should be allowed to get closer. But under questioning from Justice John Paul Stevens on how close, he admitted that perhaps a two-foot limit may be acceptable to ensure access.
Souter asked about stalker laws, but Sekulow replied that such activity crossed the line from protected speech to illegal harassment.
